destination.title: Police Took His Phone. Then They Opened It.

short07: Even after an arrest, police cannot just open your phone.
For two centuries, officers could search the things you had on you when you were arrested.
It can hold your messages, photos, location history, and almost your whole life.
In 2014, the Supreme Court was unanimous.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: To see why this was hard, you have to understand a rule called "search incident to arrest." For a long time, the courts have allowed police, when they make a lawful arrest, to search the person and the area within their reach — without a separate warrant .
Then, in 2014, the Supreme Court gave an answer so blunt it became famous: if the police want to search your phone, get a warrant .
For two hundred years, the law had a simple rule: when the police arrest you, they can search what is on you — your pockets, your wallet, whatever you are carrying — without a warrant .
In 2009, a man named David Riley is pulled over in San Diego, California.
By 2014, searching the device could quietly become a search of a life that is kept half in your pocket and half in the cloud .
In 2014, the Supreme Court ruled, and not one justice dissented .
The opinion was written by Chief Justice John Roberts, and its core was simple: the police generally may not search the digital contents of a cell phone seized during an arrest without a warrant .
The Court did not say the police can never see what is on your phone.
After 2014, the most personal object most people own could not be cracked open by the police just because they had been arrested.

shorts.angle: Get a warrant came with an off switch and a hard edge: in a real emergency police still do not wait, and the ruling only guarded the data you put in the phone yourself.
shorts.type: A — second-person threat ('this can reach you')
shorts.avoids: Both existing Shorts land on the unanimous 2014 holding that searching a phone needs a warrant. Neither says the Court left an emergency door open, or that the protection stops at the contents you chose to put there and says almost nothing about what the phone generates on its own.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Who owns the location trail the phone sends out by itself, and what the Court said about it four years later.
shorts.loop_join: L5 says almost nobody read far enough, and L1 explains why on the restart: three words landed and everyone stopped reading there.

lines.text: Get a warrant. Three words from the Supreme Court, and everyone stopped reading there.
source_lines: The ruling came down to three words that are now quoted constantly: get a warrant

lines.text: The Court did not say police can never see what is on your phone. It said they have to go to a judge, show probable cause, and get one.
source_lines: The Court did not say the police can never see what is on your phone. It said they have to do what the Constitution normally requires for something this private: go to a judge, show probable cause, and get a warrant

lines.text: And it left a door open. In a true emergency, a bomb, a kidnapping, a child in danger, police can still act without waiting. It protects your phone. It does not make it a shield.
source_lines: The Court left one important door open. In a true emergency — a bomb, a kidnapping, a child in danger — the police can still act without waiting for a warrant
The rule protects your phone. It does not turn it into a shield.

lines.text: Then look at what it actually guarded. The messages, the photos, the files you put there on purpose. Not what your phone creates on its own and hands to your carrier.
source_lines: It protects the contents of the phone — the messages, the photos, the files you can see when you unlock it. It assumes the private thing is the data you put there on purpose.
Every few minutes, it tells the nearest tower where it is.

lines.text: You never type that trail. You never see it. And almost nobody read far enough into the ruling to find out who owns it.
